reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: A rare but almost uniformly fatal complication caused by viable donor T lymphocytes engrafting and attacking recipient tissues
Typically appears one to six weeks after transfusion with fever, a maculopapular rash, diarrhoea, hepatitis, and progressive pancytopenia
Marrow aplasia distinguishes it from graft-versus-host disease after stem cell transplant, where the graft spares recipient marrow
Highest risk in severely immunocompromised recipients and when donor and recipient share an HLA haplotype, as with directed donations from blood relatives
Gamma or X-ray irradiation of cellular components to inactivate donor lymphocytes is the cornerstone of prevention; leukoreduction alone is insufficient
Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy and by demonstrating donor-derived lymphocytes or chimerism in the recipient
Established disease responds poorly to immunosuppression, so prevention through irradiation of at-risk transfusions is paramount
reference.pathophysiology: TA-GVHD occurs when immunologically competent donor T lymphocytes contained in a cellular blood component are not eliminated by the recipient's immune system and instead engraft, proliferate, and mount an immune attack against host tissues bearing foreign HLA antigens. This happens when the recipient is profoundly immunosuppressed or when the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype shared with the recipient, so the recipient fails to recognise the donor cells as foreign. The activated donor lymphocytes target skin, gut, liver, and bone marrow, with marrow involvement producing the aplasia that drives the high mortality.
additionalDifferentials: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or other drug eruptions
Viral infection with rash and cytopenias
Marrow failure or aplastic anaemia from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing characteristic histology of graft-versus-host disease
Full blood count documenting progressive pancytopenia
HLA typing and detection of donor lymphocyte chimerism in blood or affected tissue
Bone marrow examination showing hypoplasia or aplasia
redFlags: Fever, rash, diarrhoea, and falling blood counts within weeks of transfusion in an at-risk patient
Any cellular transfusion given without irradiation to a severely immunocompromised recipient or from a first-degree relative
Rapid multi-organ deterioration requiring urgent haematology involvement
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is extremely poor once established, with mortality generally exceeding ninety per cent largely from marrow aplasia and infection; the emphasis therefore lies entirely on prevention by irradiating cellular components for at-risk patients.
pitfalls: Failing to irradiate cellular components for immunocompromised recipients or directed family donations
Assuming leukoreduction alone prevents the disease
Attributing the rash, diarrhoea, and cytopenias to drugs or infection and delaying recognition
Not flagging patients who require lifelong irradiated components in their transfusion records
